extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry/literary criticism; general readers practising close reading
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating lyric poems by scrutinising reader responses (imagery, diction, rhythm, tone, unity, etc.) and identifying legitimate vs illegitimate critical expectations. Emphasises context-sensitive judgement rather than fixed canons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mnemonic pull / memorability
rubrics_metrics.description: The mnemonic pull (memorability) of a poem governs readers' reactions and can make a poem popular or familiar even when its tonal ground is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that strong memorability is a legitimate feature but may not indicate depth or clear tonal basis; it can distort judgement when taken as sole evidence of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery / the mental-picture test
rubrics_metrics.description: If the test of the mental picture arising in the reader's mind from the poet's words is a test at all, the poem is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poem produces vivid mental images; note that repetition of the same verbal image can tire, and that verbal images do not always match readers' visualising habits. Images often intensify both strong and weak poems (making good better, bad worse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery as sign of reader engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' visual images are often signs of how they are getting on with the poem rather than a direct means the poet uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat readers' idiosyncratic visualisations (e.g., seeing a cloud with a pencil) as evidence of individual response, not necessarily of poetic success or failure; some readers approach poetry visually and may compensate elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against prescriptive human-interest requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The preconception that a poem must show 'human interest' (e.g., men and their affairs) is illegitimate; 'The proper study of mankind is man' is not a necessary rule for poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a poem interests readers in itself; absence of explicit human figures does not make a poem 'dead' — poems are 'tissues of human impulses' even without direct human reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words having inherent 'character' (rejected presupposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that words in themselves have fixed characters (ugly, beautiful, delicate, weighty) and that a poem's subject prescribes a dictionary selection is unsound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess words by their use in context; resist treating individual words as intrinsically appropriate or inappropriate apart from their function within the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alliteration and sonic devices evaluated in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Alliteration and similar devices may be effective (e.g., suggesting drifting cloud) but must be judged by their place and function in the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying external canons of euphony; consider whether sound-patterns co-operate with other lines and the poem's ends rather than condemning certain consonant combinations out of context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosaicism / prosaic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often accuse certain words of being 'prosaic' (e.g., 'puzzle', 'sidle', 'encroachments'), treating the term 'prosaic' as equivalent to 'unsatisfactory'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise 'prosaic' as a subjective general reproach; in absence of precise theory, treat it as a signal to examine whether the diction serves the poem's development rather than as absolute condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cacophony / euphony considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of ugliness of certain sound combinations (cacophony) are common, but no sound can be judged apart from its context and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply broad rules banning certain sound clusters; attempt to justify sound-effects by showing how they contribute to the poem's overall design or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about onomatopoeia
rubrics_metrics.description: Most alleged instances of onomatopoeia are imaginary; they are more cases of suggestion than literal imitation of sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of praising a line solely for supposed onomatopoeic mimicry; emphasise the suggestive power of language rather than literal sound imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between subject and verse movement (illegitimate demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand that the movement of a poem's verse must imitate the visible movement of its subject (e.g., a cloud) is a typical but illegitimate technical expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can be a merit if the poet intends and requires it, but it is not a defect if omitted; whether verse motion corresponds to subject depends on poet's inducements and reader's willingness to accept the correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter/rhythm judged relative to reader's uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: The rhythm of words is not independent of the way the reader chooses to take them; perceived correspondence or mismatch may depend on reader's receptivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for reader variation when assessing metrical suitability; do not treat isolated metrical features as decisive without considering their effect in performance and pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegitimate comparisons with canonical poems/poets
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate comparison with a famous poem (e.g., Shelley's 'The Cloud') is commonly unfair and can prejudice judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid automatic benchmarking against canonical works; compare only when relevant and with attention to different aims, tones, and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to romantic animism/personification (contested)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some readers object to animistic personification (clouds 'puzzling' cattle) as ugliness or falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that anthropomorphism is a stylistic choice; physical implausibility does not automatically invalidate metaphorical intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of Latin and Anglo-Saxon words (rejected presupposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that mixing words of Latin and Anglo-Saxon origin is 'scarcely happy' is widespread but unfounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question such received doctrines; word-origin prejudice is not a reliable aesthetic rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone-shift and unity (endings / last lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden change of tone (e.g., in stanza six) or declamatory final lines can spoil a poem's earlier delicacy and unity, creating bathos or anti-climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between accidental incoherence and deliberate tonal shift; consider whether the change is intended to alter meaning or mood before condemning it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificiality / forced conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: An impression that phrases are 'strung together' or that the poem is 'full of conceits' indicates artificiality and insincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat forcedness as a valid ground for criticism if diction and metaphor feel contrived rather than organically emergent from the poem's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity and incomprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poems appear incomprehensible on first readings; obscurity may be a legitimate poetic device or a flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for careful study to reveal meanings; but persistent vagueness, lack of anchors, or meaningless phrasing are defensible reasons for negative judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal-physical plausibility not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers sometimes object on geometrical/physical grounds (e.g., a cloud cannot 'shake its shadow at the sun'), but such literal impossibilities do not necessarily invalidate poetic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret metaphorically where plausible; check whether a literal reading is the only reasonable option before dismissing a line on physics alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Last-line tone: perfunctory regret vs genuine transition
rubrics_metrics.description: The final lines can read as perfunctory/regretful moralising or as signaling a genuine emotional or metaphysical transition (e.g., transitoriness vs surviving glory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the last lines grow organically from preceding material or are tacked-on moralising; judge their success by their integration with earlier stanzas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for vivid presentation/atmosphere (illegitimate prescription)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often expect vivid presentation or atmosphere from all poetry; prescribing such features is unreasonable because poets may deliberately avoid them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept diversity of aims: some poems aim for restraint or reflection rather than sensory rapture; criticism should not impose a single expected mood on all poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for personal emotion / requirement of 'rapture' (illegitimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some readers demand personal emotion or 'rapture' as a necessary quality; this conflates intensity with quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish intensity of feeling from poetic worth; absence of overt rapture does not prove failure if the poem accomplishes other ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of sincerity and bareness of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity, simplicity, probability and even bareness of diction can be merits; bare language may give intensity and seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that lack of ornate diction or 'pretty images' can be an aesthetic choice that strengthens a poem's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythmic attractiveness vs endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem's rhythm might be immediately attractive (likened to a 'jazz tune') yet have limited repeat value or depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate pleasing surface rhythm from sustained poetic worth; consider whether rhythmic charm masks superficiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of paraphrase and reductive summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers frequently paraphrase lines and reduce them to simplistic statements (e.g., turning a phrase into a banal paraphrase), which can mislead judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reductive paraphrase as the primary critical tool; attend to diction, structure, and tone rather than collapsing lines into banal prose equivalents.
